title.narrative: AWESOME (Advancing Women’s Engagement: Strengthening Opportunities to Mobilise for Equality)

description.narrative: A 5 year advocacy programme to support women’s movements in Ethiopia, Kenya and Uganda to be strengthened, less fragmented and more representative of diverse groups of women, including women with disabilities. These stronger women’s movements will contribute to strong women leaders at all levels, and the prevention and elimination of sexual and gender based violence (SGBV) against women and girls.

description.narrative: Number of policy and civil society spaces created, attended or facilitated to create space for CSO demands.

comment.narrative: Baseline indicator is zero because the target refers to policy and advocacy spaces created, attended or facilitated under AWESOME. Although influencing opportunities change each year and we’ll update the advocacy calendar as the programme progresses, there are some that will remain constant throughout the 5 years because these are set days in the human rights calendar. This is in addition to, from 2022, the AUC and ACHPR meetings which happen in January, April and November each year.

In Year 1, Womankind facilitated the participation of the consortium partners in the 16 days of activism through the creation of the 16 Days Podcast which was a co-curation of a 5-part podcast series to address femicide and intersecting thematic areas together with the African Women’s Communication and Development Network (FEMNET). Episodes were released on specific days during 16 Days of Activism related to their significance in the context of women’s rights and feminist organising. On 3rd December, the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, the podcast on Femicide and Women with Disabilities featured partner EWDNA. On 10th December, International Human Rights Day the podcast on Femicide and Women’s Political Leadership featured partner FOWODE. The podcasts also provided a space in which to amplify the work of the two organisations on the issue of femicide. Consortium partners EWDNA and FIDA- Kenya further contributed to the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affair’s Task Force for Gender Equality and Women’s Rights annual Orange the World campaign against gender-based violence (GBV) contributing stories on strategies the organisations use to address SGBV. In year 2, In 2022 WK facilitated consortium partners participation in The Sexual Violence Research Initiative Forum (The SVRI) . The SVRI is the world’s largest network on research on violence against women (VAW) and violence against children (VAC). The forum was an opportunity to AWESOME to engage in cross-movements spaces, build alliances with like-minded organisations, and amplify the work that AWESOME partners are doing at country level. AWESOME organised a participant-led event, 'Intersectional feminist movement strengthening and disability inclusion: Experiences from Kenya, Uganda and Ethiopia drawing from the AWESOME consortium.' Partners had the opportunity to talk about their work, drawing from the first two years of implementation, and the AWESOME learning event. Eight representatives from the AWESOME consortium attended the forum this included six representatives from six consortium partners. Representatives from SWDA were unable to attend as they were not able to get their visas on time despite their best efforts. WK also facilitated a process for AWEOSOME consortium members to work strategically toward a joint action at Africa Commission for Human and Peoples Rights (ACHPR), in Gambia. WK coordinated the drafting of a joint statement to the ACHPR which . The joint statement was delivered orally to the Commission by AWESOME consortium partner FIDA-Kenya at the Commission’s 73rd Public Ordinary Session, in Banjul Gambia. The joint statement highlighted the key learnings from AWESOME on the intersection between VAW and the low numbers of women in political leadership. WK also facilitated participation of FIDA-Kenya in The Forum on the Participation of NGOs in the Ordinary Sessions of the African Commission (the NGOs Forum). The AWESOME consortium used this opportunity to disseminate learnings and experiences from the AWESOME consortium, strengthen cross-movement collaboration with CSOs working on WPL and VAW in the three AWESOME countries and establish relationships with key policymakers and commissioners of the African Union and ACPHR to advance the consortium’s key policy objectives. In the first half of Y3, Womankind facilitated the participation of Representatives from the seven partners of the AWESOME consortium attended the 67th Session of the Commission on the Status of Women, which took place in New York (USA) between the 6 and 17 of March 2023. Due to our parallel event being allocated to the second week by the Commission, the AWESOME delegation travelled to New York from the 11th until the 18th of March. The parallel event was on the topic of “Rural Girls’ and Women’s Feminist Movement Strengthening: Southern WROs Experiences”, and partners shared their experiences as mainstream and disabled WROs in relation to their work with diverse women based in rural areas in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Uganda under the AWESOME project. Panellists discussed their work in responding to sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) and engagement in decision-making spaces on women’s participation and leadership, to enhance gender equality and empowerment among girls and women in their communities. A month after the event, we held an online session with all AWESOME attendees to gather feedback and reflect on how it went and share best practices and lessons learnt. All participants highlighted the importance of attending this very strategic space, and that it provided a great opportunity for advocacy and networking. For example, Dibabe from EWDNA mentioned how they had the opportunity to meet with the Ministry and talk about the issue of SGBV in Ethiopia, Jackline from WCC explained how they had a chat with a representative from Microsoft which showed interested in partnering with them for an ICT project, and Betty from NUWODU had the chance to engage with Ugandan ministries and other government stakeholders. In addition, Womankind was part of the Women’s Rights Caucus (WRC) and engaged in several of their working groups prior to the conference and was able to influence WRC for the accessibility of its messaging. In the same session, partners reported that they appreciated the autonomy to choose how their experience of CSW will be; meaning they had the freedom to choose the events they wanted and exploring the opportunities that are relevant to their work, and this also influences how spaces are created for partners to engage in strategic spaces in ways that are useful and relevant for their work. At this debrief session, partners also discussed lessons learnt and areas for improvement. It was agreed that, although partners had engaged with many actors during CSW, more focus could have been put in engaging with other organisations and government representatives in each of the three countries prior to the conference. It was agreed that partners would lead on this work in their own countries the following years, and Womankind would continue to engage with the Women’s Rights Caucus (WRC).

In years 3-5, Womankind created space for CSO demands at 8 international advocacy/influencing spaces. The UN CSW and the African Union ACHPR were key influencing spaces. For example, in year 5 AWESOME co-convened a side event with FAWE with 50 attendees. We used the event to deliver a call to action on women's participation and leadership, including the violence faced by women in politics. Our policy brief on violence against women in politics had 4650 views and 250 engagements on X. Womankind contributed technical support and shared our ECOSOC status to help with partnership-wide registrations, travel and coordination. We faced some backlash from anti-rights groups in attendance, but partners responded swiftly. Partners fed-back that participation at CSW helps with their networking, mobilising support and for fundraising sustainability.

Annual targets: 1 space in year 1 (Global/International), 3 spaces in year 2 (at least one African Union and one Global/International), 2 spaces in year 3 (at least one African Union and one Global/International), 3 spaces in year 4 (at least one African Union, one Global/International and one London visit), 3 spaces in year 5 (at least one African Union, one Global/International and one London visit), Target by end of AWESOME: 12 policy and civil society spaces created, attended or facilitated

description.narrative: Number of pieces of content produced that amplify the voices of diverse women (SGBV focus, although the 2 themes intersect and we will often cover both)

comment.narrative: Comment: No content has been produced within AWESOME yet (so the baseline value is 0). Of the 26 pieces of Womankind’s written media content in Jan 2020 - April 2021 (all blogs, news, comment pieces), our internal analysis found that 31% amplified the voices of women and partners, and 27% amplified the voices of women who are marginalised (WWD, young women, and LBTQI+ women).

In years 3-5, Womankind launched 3 media pieces to create space for CSO demands on SGBV and women's leadership (1 on SGBV and 2 on participation and leadership). For example, Womankind launched a coffee table book in Oct'25, 'Seeds of Change', which speaks to agenda setting and documenting partner stories (www.womankind.org.uk/the-awesome-programme-launches-new-book-of-stories-seeds-of-change/). It is a collection of stories of women and girls in Kenya, Ethiopia and Uganda from the past 5 years. The book mirrors the struggles, victories, and ongoing journey of women and girls who refuse to be silenced. It is also a reflection of the solidarity of partners, communities, and donors who believe that real change happens when power is shared, voices are amplified, and justice is pursued with persistence and determination. By gathering these stories, we are reminded that narratives are powerful tools for change. They help us see the human face behind statistics, they connect us to lived realities, and they inspire us to act. Wider agenda setting work continued in year 5 around #SafeInEverySpace focused on TFGBV and #SafeAtWork focused on decent work and the ILO C190 agenda. There was also work to amplify women's demands from CSW69 including on a violence against women in politics.

Year 1:"Womankind facilitated the participation of consortium partners in the 16 Days of Activism through the creation of a 16 Days Podcast. This was a co-curation of a 5-part podcast series to address femicide and intersecting thematic areas, together with the African Women’s Communication and Development Network (FEMNET). Episodes were released on specific days during 16 Days of Activism related to their significance in the context of women’s rights and feminist organising. On 3rd December, the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, the podcast on Femicide and Women with Disabilities featured partner EWDNA. On 10th December, International Human Rights Day the podcast on Femicide and Women’s Political Leadership featured partner FOWODE. The podcasts also provided a space in which to amplify the work of the two organisations on the issue of femicide.We also published an ILO Brief and blog, which consulted partners and they contributed to the content, but was not co-authored by partners so does not meet our definitions for this indicator."Year 2: Womankind aunched the website for the AWESOME consortium, which provides an overview of the programme, as well as different blogs and other resources developed by the consortium partners. The website sits within Womankind's domain, ensuring that the AWESOME's website can benefit from the visits to the long-established Womankind's website.

Comment: 3 pieces of content in total. 100% will amplify the voices of diverse women, and will have challenged Womankind to think differently about the content we produce more broadly.By media that amplify voices we mean a piece of media/communications content, which has either a) direct quotes from a partner or a woman involved in the work, or b) the piece was authored by partners, or c) video content is of a woman speaking of her experiences. Not included in this definition would be when there is content that mentions partner organisations, or types of women and the issues they face, but without quotes or authorship.When we say that we want to amplify the voices of ‘diverse women’ we refer to the women that Womankind and partners are working with, including (and recognising that many women involved cross intersections of these groups) women with disabilities, internally displaced women, young women, aspiring and newly elected women leaders, women in rural areas, women industrial workers, women affected by conflict, survivors of SGBV, community leaders (not necessarily elected or aspirants but functioning in different spaces), informal workers (working on the fringes of the industrial zones and reached through the programme in Ethiopia for example), and WHRDs (includes women working within partner organisations).

title.narrative: Women's rights organisation (WRO) partners in the AWESOME Alliance with strengthened capacities
Number of women's rights organisation (WRO) partners in the AWESOME Alliance with strengthened capacities

comment.narrative: Womankind recognises that strengthening women’s organisations is crucial in maintaining and widening the space for voice, visibility, advocacy and evidence about violations of women’s rights in their regions. We also acknowledge that “L&A capacities” is a very subjective statement in terms of both the nature and the magnitude of change. By increased capacities we mean all types of capacity building and support offered through AWESOME (such as the FOCS funding, safeguarding training, MEL training, Disability and Inclusion training etc).Partners have varying L&A capacity. In Ethiopia, the previous government prohibited L&A activities consequently partners SWDA, and EWDNA, Ethiopia have limited experience in this regard. However with opening up of civic space in Ethiopia, SWDA and EWDNA have began conduct advocacy and lobbying on WPL and VAW, however their participation in international and regional advocacy has been limited. In Kenya and Uganda partners have extensive experience in L&A on WPL and VAW particularly towards their national governments. Mainstream WRO Fida (Kenya) and FOWODE (Uganda) have extensive regional and international lobby experience. However the movements are fragmented and are not always inclusive particularly of WWDs.

Strengthened intersectional women’s movements - voice, representation, accountability, collaboration and networking. i) In each of the focus countries partners are truly inclusive and representative of diverse groups of women, drawing on expertise and experiences of DWROs and WWDs to in ii) Programme partners have capacity meaningfully engage in lobby and advocacy at national, regional and international spaces to improve laws on WPL and SGBV and ensure that these laws take into account the concerns of WWDs. With regards to Womankind's strengthened capacity, that will be around disability inclusion in practice and we are currently taking steps towards this in AWESOME but also more broadly organisation-wise. Womankind has experience working with DWROs, however internal capacity and inclusion needs to the improved with regards to policies and practice.

In progress. AWESOME is supporting capacity strengthening of all partners through FOCS funding, and through cross-partner collaboration. FOCS: Partners continue to benefit from FOCS funds provided in Y1 and Y2. For example, in 2024 WCC finalised their Strategic Plan 2024-29 (partly funded by FOCS in previous years). EWDNA and SWDA continue to benefit from the staff training on project management and advocacy to all staff, ensuring enhanced project management and advocacy capacities and organisational sustainability. FOWODE carried a review and documentation of their implementation models, to assess their relevance, effectiveness, sustainability, and scalability in advancing gender equality and women’s leadership in Uganda. Key models evaluated include Civic Education, Gender Action Learning Systems (GALS), Gender Leadership Clubs (GLCs), and Leadership Advisory Desks (LADs). Funding for this was provided in 2023, but work was delayed to 2024 due to delays in finding a suitable consultant. Example of cross-partner collaboration include: Womankind now has an organisational workplan to improve accessibility and inclusion, thanks to DWRO engagement. FIDA has also improved their approach to inclusion, and this year sought support from WCC to nominate deaf women to participate in the National Women’s Rights Conference. Partners' strengthened capacities were particularly evidenced this year by leading engagements for the fist time: EWDNA hosted the AWESOME 3 day learning event as their first cross-country meeting, and FOWODE led advocacy and logistics for all partners attending the ACHPR.

Strengthened intersectional women’s movements - voice, representation, accountability, collaboration and networking. i)In each of the focus countries partners are truly inclusive and representative of diverse groups of women, drawing on expertise and experiences of DWROs and WWDs to inii)Programme partners have capacity meaningfully engage in lobby and advocacy at national, regional and international spaces to improve laws on WPL and SGBV and ensure that these laws take into account the concerns of WWDs.With regards to Womankind's strengthened capacity, that will be around disability inclusion in practice and we are currently taking steps towards this in AWESOME but also more broadly organisation-wise. Womankind has experience working with DWROs, however internal capacity and inclusion needs to the improved with regards to policies and practice.

Over 5 years, all 6 women-led WRO partners (100%) have significatly strengthened their organisational capacities as WROs engaged in advocacy. The two main routes for strengthening were: 1) Individual partner plans and funding for feminist organisational capacity strengthening; and 2) Consortia-wide capacity strengthening efforts. At the individual organisation level, from the outset, each partner worked to define their own context- and organisation-specific capacity priorities, with dedicated funding to address these gaps. Partners were encouraged to recognize that strong organisations are able to strongly advocate, so partners therefore took diverse paths towards advocacy capacity strengthening dependent on their expertise, contexts and opportunities. Priorities included strengthening skills in feminist advocacy, safeguarding, monitoring and evaluation, and disability inclusion. At the consortium level, annual in-person learning events, quarterly Joint Consortium Steering Committee (JCSC) meetings, and cross-country participation in international advocacy spaces provided structured spaces for shared learning, adaptive management, and alignment of advocacy strategies across diverse country contexts. Our feminist practice of rotational leadership of these events meant that organisations built capacity in hosting international events and leading in international advocacy spaces (such as the AU ACHPR).As a result, partners have been able to engage in national dialogue processes and labour institutions (Ethiopia); expanded reach into new counties and established growing pipelines of aspirant women leaders (Kenya); strengthened roles as convenors of feminist coalitions (Uganda); and built practices around disability accessibility and inclusion (Womankind). In Ethiopia, EWDNA has strengthened their organisational capacity with membership by WWDs increasing by 360% in just 5 years. A key learning has been the value of investing in capacity strengthening from the first years of the programme. Partners have been able to test, explore and build on capacities over 5 years and this has created valuable time to reflect on what is working and to pivot when needed.

Strengthened intersectional women’s movements - voice, representation, accountability, collaboration and networking. i) In each of the focus countries partners are truly inclusive and representative of diverse groups of women, drawing on expertise and experiences of DWROs and WWDs to in ii) Programme partners have capacity meaningfully engage in lobby and advocacy at national, regional and international spaces to improve laws on WPL and SGBV and ensure that these laws take into account the concerns of WWDs. With regards to Womankind's strengthened capacity, that will be around disability inclusion in practice and we are currently taking steps towards this in AWESOME but also more broadly organisation-wise. Womankind has experience working with DWROs, however internal capacity and inclusion needs to the improved with regards to policies and practice.

To contribute to increasing capacities of WROs in year one all AWESOME partners received funding for Feminist Organisational Capacity Strengthening (FOCS). Year two saw partners using the FOCs funding to perform activities to strengthen their capacities and increase sustainability of their organisations. EWDNA used the funding for the development of an M&E manual to guide monitoring and learning of the organisation, EWDNA also used the funding to train staff on different methods of data collection and best practices with regards to report writing. The development of the M&E manual and the training on the data collection will enable EWDNA to conduct more feminist MEL which centres not just the organisation but its constituents as well. The data collected with the skills acquired will be used for evidence-based advocacy and fund raising. EWDNA staff also received training in advocacy which is useful as it is only recently that the Ethiopia government opened the space for advocacy. EWDNA has also used the funding for the development of members data management system to keep track of its growing membership.SWDA used the FOCs funding to update her existing code of conduct and safeguarding policies to include anti-harassment and HIV/AIDS awareness. SWDA also updated her Gender Policy to incorporate accountability mechanisms to their constituencies. SWDA staff underwent trainings on the newly updated policies and MEL. SWDA and EWDNA also held an annual programme review meeting with 10 SWDA staff and 10 EWDNA staff. Both partners discussed their successes, challenges, lessons learned during the reporting period, and plans to work together in 2023.In Kenya WCC used their FOCs funding to start consultation for the development of their new strategic plan. The strategic plan that WCC has was last renewed in 2016 and needs revision in the light of global and country changes. FIDA-Kenya used their FOCs funding to support to their biannual Results Based Management (RBM). RBM has become a key priority for FIDA in its programming. FIDA-Kenya hopes her investments in RBM will increase organisational effectiveness, efficiency and ensure that results are achieved in a timely and quality manner.In Uganda, NUWODU used their FOCs funding to develop a resource mobilisation strategy that will allow her to leverage her position as an umbrella organisation for GwDs and WwDs by mobilising resources to ensure a society where GwDs and WwDs live dignified lives. This is important particularly as DWROs have historically not been recipients of statutory and institutional grants.In August 2022 in Uganda, the AWESOME consortium partners held a learning event and interrogated questions around feminism and disability inclusion within the context of the AWESOME programme hosted by NUWODU. The objective of the learning event was to closely examine both inclusion and exclusion of women with disabilities in feminist and women’s rights movements, and specifically, to understand patterns of exclusion, the forces driving this exclusion and how inclusion is understood by both mainstream women’s rights organisations and disability women’s rights organisations. The discussions and learnings from this event were consolidated in a learning event report that contains reflections, experiences, and strategies on disability inclusion within the AWESOME consortium. The hope is that these learnings and conversations about disability, inclusion, and feminism, grounded in lived experience, will contribute to a more inclusive practice within the programme but also in the wider women’s movement.WK continues to work closely with partners to strengthen their capacity on Aidstream and other IATI-related platforms. All partners have reported challenges with using Aidstream especially the first two years of the project. These challenges have included the platforms not being user friendly, needing a lot of time and resources to be able to navigate both the platform, and lack of accessibility due to connectivity issues. To support in this area WK has had regular one-to-onemeetings with all partners and developed several step-by-step guidelines that are specific for the AWESOME programme. All partners have reported increased capacity and knowledge to use the Aidstream platform.

Strengthened intersectional women’s movements - voice, representation, accountability, collaboration and networking. i) In each of the focus countries partners are truly inclusive and representative of diverse groups of women, drawing on expertise and experiences of DWROs and WWDs to in ii) Programme partners have capacity meaningfully engage in lobby and advocacy at national, regional and international spaces to improve laws on WPL and SGBV and ensure that these laws take into account the concerns of WWDs. With regards to Womankind's strengthened capacity, that will be around disability inclusion in practice and we are currently taking steps towards this in AWESOME but also more broadly organisation-wise. Womankind has experience working with DWROs, however internal capacity and inclusion needs to the improved with regards to policies and practice.

We are not focusing only on lobby and advocacy capacities, but generally in supporting organisations to get stronger. We work in the assumption that stronger organisations, and stronger coalitions, have better capacity to do advocacy and lobbying. Accessibility and inclusion: We have seen improvements across the consortium, with mainstream organisations being more radically inclusive of women with disabilities. For instance, in Kenya, FIDA is taking accessibility seriously, with some tangible changes such as sign language interpretation at their events and accessible formats for printed documents, inclusivity being at the core of their mobilisation and beneficiaries' selection strategies or participating in activities organised by WCC with a focus on learning best practices for accessibility and advocating for the rights of WWDs. In Uganda, FOWODE’s groups’ selection criteria, inclusion was an aspect deliberately included to ensure that often-unheard voices, such as those of PWDs, and they prioritise trainers with disabilities, when possible, to deliver sessions. In Ethiopia, SWDA is actively reaching out to PWDs to join their activities and started disaggregating data by disability to ensure inclusive MEL. At Womankind, we continue to learn from partners ways in which we can improve our accessibility and inclusion practices. Thanks to continued engagement with and feedback from partners, we have made tangible changes to our ways of working to ensure we are accessible and inclusive. Some of these changes include accessible communications and materials (closed captioning at meetings, translation to braille, sign language interpretation for events), accessibility built into budgets, engagement with PWDs in advance of any activity or travel to ensure we are able to implement any reasonable accommodation. Staff from WCC and EWDNA have mentioned on different occasions that they appreciate WK’s approach of giving the opportunity to include a personal assistant for any national or international travel when needed, and they felt this was very good practice from an accessibility and inclusion perspective. Partly thanks to the learnings from the AWESOME consortium, Womankind created the Accessibility and Inclusion working group, to improve our approach to accessibility and be actively and truly accessible. This cross-organisational group is led by WK’s AWESOME programme officer, and they meet monthly to look at ways in which processes and ways of working can be improved with an intersectional and feminist approach to accessibly and inclusion. Coalition strengthening: Consortium partners are increasingly working together, and there are several in-country initiatives and joint activities. In September 2023, AWESOME partners came together in Nairobi (Kenya) for a learning event to explore ways in which partners are contributing to pathways for Women’s Political Leadership and Participation in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Uganda. This space provided partners with the opportunity to exchange practices, challenges and lessons learnt, promoting cross-country learning. Consortium partners have highlighted in the past the importance of in-person spaces for coalition building and regional movement strengthening. Though three in-person spaces are facilitated each year under AWESOME (international and regional advocacy spaces, and the learning event) and this has been reported by partners as key moments that have strengthened their work and cross-consortium relationships, it is recognised that more in-person international and regional opportunities should be provided to truly support regional feminist movement strengthening. Though more in-person engagement is outside of the scope of AWESOME, we continue to support and promote coalition strengthening through Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL): We continue to have regular MEL sessions with all consortium partners, where we discuss specific topics related to monitoring, evaluation and learning. These sessions provide a space for sharing and learning from each other, collectively strengthening the MEL capacity of consortium members. In the earlier stages of the programme, partners would have more practical questions around MEL frameworks, data disaggregation, IATI, reporting, and so on, and these sessions provided a space for all MEL leads to come in and ask questions on areas that they identified needing support or capacity strengthening – particularly necessitated by the MFA’s MEL expectations. However, as the programme advanced, it seemed partners were more confident and needed less day-to-day support, so attendance to the sessions started to decrease in early 2023. We carried out a consultation with partners on the relevance of having these spaces monthly, and it was collectively decided that these spaces were still relevant, however frequency should be decreased to quarterly, and instead of focusing only on issues, we could also collectively identify MEL topics that were relevant for the consortium to explore, such as measuring attitudinal change or avoid double counting when reporting. Though this space will have a focus on wider feminist MEL topics, we still hold space for discussing issues and learnings related to reporting requirements and feedback. Since the meetings started happening quarterly, active attendance has increased again, and partners continue to report these spaces as useful and relevant. The use of the Aidstream to publish data at the International Aid Transparency Initiative (IATI) platform has been raised as a challenge by most partners since the start of the programme. Thanks to the ongoing 1-to-1 sessions with partners and tailored step by step guidelines developed by WK’s team, it has been reported that capacity around the use of Aidstream, IATI, and other related platforms has been strengthened, with partners needing less 1-to-1 support. Though partners report increased knowledge on how to use the platform, there are ongoing challenges around how data needs to be reported to comply with donor requirements, which means WK team still does regular thorough reviews of all data added and sends feedback for partners to review and update. In Year 3 we carried out a Mid-Term Review, supported by Southern Hemisphere consultancy. All partners contributed to creating the Terms of Reference and then participated in the review through a mixture of in-person and online spaces. We tried to emphasize feminist MEL approaches throughout and centring partners’ experiences and perspectives, using an outcome harvesting approach, triangulated with document reviews, interviews and focus group discussions in all three countries. The findings of the review validated AWESOME’s theory of change and highlighted numerous strong practices by each partner to strengthening the women’s movement. Feminist Organisational Capacity Strengthening (FOCS): In Year 3, partners received the second tranche of their FOCS funding to use in areas identified by them as needing capacity strengthening. Women Challenged to Challenge (WCC): WCC has used their Year 3 FOCS funding to improve the resource mobilisation capacity of their staff, supporting the sustainability of the organisation and their work. Sixteen people from their staff, executive committee and community resource persons attended the 2-day training, and covered topics such as sustainability, resource mobilisation process, proposal development and pitching amongst others. WCC has reported that this training has improved the capacity of their staff, specially of those team members that did not have any prior experience in resource mobilisation and will go a long way in ensuring WCC’s sustainability. FIDA: FIDA-Kenya developed its new strategic plan 2023-2027. It was imperative for FIDA-Kenya secretariat and board members to comprehend and acquaint themselves with the plan before its launch and execution. The capacity of 40 personnel was enhanced through the unpackaging of the plan by a consultant. This activity was done at FIDA-Kenya’s bi-annual Results Based Management meeting at Stoni-Athi resort on the 17th-20th July 2023. Ethiopian Women with Disabilities National Association (EWDNA): EWDNA has used their FOCS funding to provide capacity strengthening for their staff; this included training on Transitional Justice, as the Ethiopian government is planning to undertake a transitional justice approach following conflicts in the country, EWDNA staff received training to learn about the process and identify areas for advocacy; they also carried a 5-day training on project management for project staff, and has planned a training on Peachtree accounting to finance staff which has been postponed into 2024 due to time constraints. Forum for Women in Democracy (FOWODE): FOWODE used their FOCS funding to review and document their implementation models. As the organisation continues to grow into a resilient and strategic player in the civic space ecosystem, their focus continues to be finding innovative and impact-reaching approaches that foster communities of hope with the agency, financial resources, and influence to drive their own change. Thus, the organisation planned a review and modification of the implementation models, through a thorough critique on the models’ ability to deliver on FOWODE’s objectives and organisational mandate. The process includes benchmarking, interrogation and comparison of the different external models to maximise our impact. This is undergoing and will be finalised in 2024 due to delays in finding a suitable consultant.

"No target for year 1. But progress includes: In line with the agreed advocacy priorities identified during the proposal development in 2020 and the inception meeting in early 2021, Womankind convened the first Advocacy training in April 2021. The training that brought together all consortium partners, and experts on advocacy. Consortium partners discussed the current policy and advocacy landscape at national, regional, and international levels in relation to the programme’s overarching objective and thematic areas, as well as different strategies for impact. The workshop provided a space for collective learning and sharing of successful context specific advocacy strategies used by consortium partners in in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Uganda as well opportunities to collaborate and elevate advocacy priorities to regional and international advocacy forums. Womankind also led a consortium wide safeguarding training with particular consideration for disability inclusion in approach. The workshop was a space for all consortium partners to create a shared understanding of safeguarding and to develop a shared programme approach to tackling safeguarding risk, prevention, reporting, response, and learning. The workshop was attended by all consortium partner safeguarding leads and partner staff members working with individuals and involved in implementation of programme activities. Judith Adokorach of the Embassy of Netherlands in Uganda also attended the training and all embassy and MfA contacts were invited. Following the workshop, consortium-wide SEAH reporting templates and guidelines detailing where, who and when to report instances of safeguarding were developed and shared with all consortium partners. The matter of safeguarding is consistently noted at the quarterly Joint Consortium Steering Committee (JCSC) meetings alongside plans for annual refresher and update sessions.During the inception process it was recognised that there was a need to have a communications and visibility strategic framework that tied the work of the programme together across the three countries. Womankind, through a series of collaborative workshops with consortium partners, created a simple and effective visual identity and strategic communications framework that accounts for individual consortium members’ own brands while bringing consistency across diverse members’ activities.Womankind also convened a workshop on Disability and Inclusion which was attended by of the consortium partners and their staff. The workshop covered topics on understanding disability, disability and gender, international, regional and national legal and policy frameworks on disability, and disability-inclusive programme delivery."
